title: Next-generation plant-wearable sensors: materials, sensing mechanisms, and plant health monitoring
authors: K. R. Kaja; S. Hajra; Rakesh Kumar Rajaboina; Uday Kumar Khanapuram; Y. Mishra; N. Vittayakorn; Venkateswaran Vivekananthan; P. Pakawanit; J. Ventura; U. Edlund; H. Kim
abstract: Abstract Over the past decade, plant-wearable sensors have attracted significant attention due to the demand for sustainable agriculture. Conventional plant monitoring systems often suffer from delayed diagnosis, destructive testing, and poor early-stress detection. In contrast, plant-wearable sensors can continuously monitor plant physiological and biochemical activities in real time. Rapid advances in flexible electronics, biodegradable materials, bioelectronics, and self-powered sensing technologies have accelerated the development of wearable sensing systems that can be attached to plant surfaces. This review discusses recent progress in plant-wearable sensors, with particular emphasis on substrate materials, target physiological parameters, and sensing mechanisms. It first compares the substrates used in plant-attached devices with biodegradable alternatives. It then defines the key physiological targets, namely plant moisture, growth, volatile organic compounds, metabolites and agrochemical residues, and electrophysiological and stress signals. Finally, it reviews the electrochemical, resistive and capacitive, triboelectric self-powered, and optical sensing mechanisms used to measure them, together with their validation conditions. The review closes with current challenges in long-term stability, biocompatibility, large-scale deployment, and data-driven intelligent agriculture, along with future opportunities for sustainable, self-powered, multifunctional bioelectronics for smart farming applications.

title: Conformationally Adaptive Through-Space Charge Transfer TADF Polymer Dots for Bioimaging and Photodynamic Therapy
authors: Nae Aota; Xujun Qiu; Leonardo Evaristo de Sousa; Piotr de Silva; Satoshi Minakata; Zachary M. Hudson; Youhei Takeda
abstract: Abstract The rational design of materials that simultaneously enable bioimaging and photodynamic therapy remains challenging because of their incompatible design principles. Herein, we disclose the synthesis of thermally activated delayed fluorescence copolymers and the development of their polymer dots, which enable both bioimaging and photodynamic therapy without additional photosensitizing segments. The copolymers incorporate a conformationally adaptive donor−π–acceptor architecture (donor = phenoxazine, π = xanthene, and acceptor = dibenzo[a,j]phenazine) as the emissive core, providing efficient orange-to-red thermally activated delayed fluorescence emission via through-space charge transfer, while effectively suppressing severe aggregation-caused quenching, even at emitter loadings as high as 15 mol %. Photophysical studies reveal that the hydrophobic copolymer possesses an extremely narrow singlet–triplet energy gap, favoring efficient intersystem crossing and reverse intersystem crossing. The formulated polymer dots, prepared either with or without a biocompatible surfactant, retain bright orange delayed fluorescence in water and exhibit efficient cellular uptake with minimal cytotoxicity. Furthermore, the polymer dots enable lysosome-targeted cellular imaging and photodynamic therapy, exhibiting a singlet oxygen generation quantum yield of 66% under white-light irradiation. Collectively, these findings highlight a promising strategy for the development of through-space charge-transfer thermally activated delayed fluorescence-based polymer dots for multifunctional nanotheranostic applications.

title: Preoperative endoscopic indocyanine green-guided fluorescence imaging improves lymph node retrieval after radical gastrectomy
authors: Xin-Fu Song; Ming-Xu Luo; Yi-Hui Lei; Xiao-Qing Huang; Yun-Ling Zhuang
abstract: BACKGROUND Adequate lymph node (LN) retrieval is essential for accurate staging and treatment planning in gastric cancer. Conventional white-light laparoscopic D2 lymphadenectomy may miss small or fat-embedded LN. Preoperative endoscopic submucosal indocyanine green (ICG) injection combined with intraoperative near-infrared (NIR) fluorescence imaging may improve nodal visualization. However, its effects on metastatic node detection, pathological staging, and early survival remain unclear. AIM To evaluate whether ICG-NIR navigation improves nodal retrieval, staging metrics, and 12-month outcomes after laparoscopic radical gastrectomy. METHODS This single-center, retrospective cohort study included 280 patients with stage I-III gastric cancer who underwent curative-intent laparoscopic gastrectomy with D2 lymphadenectomy from July 2023 to December 2025. Patients were classified into the ICG-NIR and conventional white-light groups according to intraoperative fluorescence use. The ICG group received an endoscopic submucosal ICG injection 18-24 hours before surgery. Propensity score matching and multivariate Cox regression were used to reduce selection bias and assess survival outcomes. RESULTS The ICG group had higher total LN retrieval than the control group (42.2 ± 9.4 vs 31.4 ± 8.8, P CONCLUSION Preoperative endoscopic submucosal ICG injection with intraoperative NIR fluorescence imaging improved LN retrieval and pathological staging and was associated with better 12-month survival outcomes after laparoscopic radical gastrectomy. Longer follow-up is required before a survival benefit can be confirmed.

title: Screening of Mannose-Functionalized Gold Nanoparticles on a Lectin Target Biointerface—An SPR Study
authors: Almar Al Assaad; Laila Yazigi; Rana Bazzi; Stéphane Roux; Wilfrid Boireau
abstract: Gold nanoparticles (GNPs) are promising platforms for combining imaging and therapeutic functions, but assessing the functional accessibility of ligands remains essential for their development. Herein, we developed a tunable biointerface on a Surface Plasmon Resonance (SPR) chip to screen the interactions of mannose-functionalized gold nanoparticles (GNP-Man) with Concanavalin A (ConA), used as a “mannose-binding lectin” model. The biointerface is based on a supramolecular architecture of a self-assembled monolayer (SAM) of TADOTAGA formed on a bare gold chip, followed by a covalent grafting of mannose and the immobilization of ConA in a controlled manner. The resulting surface showed reproducible preparation, good stability, and efficient regeneration. Five GNP-Man batches with nominal Man/GNP ratios of 10, 20, 50, 100 and 200 were characterized by TEM, DLS, and UV–visible spectroscopy. A dose–response study with GNP-Man10 validated the SPR methodology, followed by a comparative screening of all formulations at 30 µg/mL. SPR responses increased with the nominal mannose density, whereas non-functionalized GNPs showed only a limited response. This proof of concept demonstrates the potential of a reusable SPR biointerface for comparative screening of GNP-Man formulations based on their functional recognition by lectins, providing a first step toward the biophysical evaluation of C-type lectin receptor (CLR)-targeted nanovectors.

title: Beyond metabolites: A wearable biointerface integrating antibody and aptamer probes for the real-time tracking of proteins in vivo
authors: Hanjia Zheng; Fatima Shafique; Alexander S. Qian; Mayank Garg; Florian Gessler; Jonathan L’Heureux Hache; Quan M. Quach; Bernardo L. Trigatti; Mahla Poudineh; Leyla Soleymani
abstract: Continuous monitoring of protein biomarkers could transform the management of acute and chronic diseases. Despite tremendous potential, wearable health monitors have remained largely limited to metabolites and small molecules. A key challenge is the limited availability of biointerfaces that reversibly track low-abundance proteins in vivo without user intervention. Here, we present the Differential Aptalyzer, a minimally invasive hydrogel microneedle platform for continuous monitoring of proteins in skin interstitial fluid. The platform combines high-affinity antibodies for selective target capture with aptamers for reversible electrochemical signal transduction. When integrated into a differential electrochemical chip and pulse-assisted sensor regeneration, this approach enables continuous monitoring of proteins in a wearable format. Using cardiac troponin I (cTnI) as a clinically relevant model analyte, Differential Aptalyzer offers a broad dynamic range (0.003 to 0.640 nanograms per milliliter) and strong specificity against interfering proteins. This platform reliably tracks both rising and falling exogenous cTnI levels injected into healthy mice, as well as endogenously elevated cTnI in a double-knockout mouse model of coronary artery disease, demonstrating its capability in continuous protein monitoring and identifying coronary artery disease cohorts.

title: Structural Design and Cyclic Reliability of Conductive Hydrogel Strain Sensors
authors: Jiajia Deng; Sheng Hu
abstract: Conductive hydrogels combine compliance, stretchability, and electrical responsiveness, enabling deformation sensing through resistance or capacitance changes and providing a material basis for wearable motion monitoring. However, toughness, low hysteresis within a single cycle, and repeatable output over prolonged cycling describe distinct properties; none alone establishes whether a sensor retains its original calibration during sustained use. Understanding this distinction requires examining how differences in the extent and timescale of recovery in load-bearing structures, conductive pathways, and interfacial contacts produce asynchronous changes in mechanical state, signal baseline, response amplitude, and loading–unloading trajectories. This review examines structural design and cyclic reliability in conductive hydrogel strain sensors, analyzing how reversible connections, interchain constraints, and interphase coupling affect mechanical dissipation and conductive-pathway rearrangement, and how device interfaces influence deformation transfer and electrical readout. It further evaluates the applicability and performance limits of structural strategies by considering crack resistance–cyclic dissipation trade-offs and the relationships between recovery time, loading schedule, strain amplitude, loading rate, hydration state, and readout conditions. Cyclic reliability should therefore be evaluated through calibration retention and strain measurement error under specified operating conditions, linking material recovery to specific measurement tasks and guiding the coordinated selection of material structures, device interfaces, and operating conditions.

title: Systematic screening reveals fluorophore-dependent fluorescence responses to porous silicon nanoparticles
authors: Han Sol Cho; Sung Cheol Kim; Ju Hyeon Park; Do-Yeon Kim; Byung Seok Cha; Dokyoung Kim
abstract: Porous silicon nanoparticles (pSiNPs) are widely used in biomedical research as biodegradable carriers that combine a large accessible pore volume with intrinsic photoluminescence. Because intrinsic emission still requires short-wavelength excitation, most imaging and theranostic designs attach or load an organic fluorophore onto the particles. However, silicon is a semiconductor, and its broad absorption manifold and dense distribution of mid-gap surface states deactivate nearby excited states through energy transfer, charge transfer, and surface-state trapping, and this quenching becomes severe once the emitter and silicon surface are in direct contact. In this study, we screened 16 organic fluorophores spanning 400–1,000 nm, including coumarins, xanthenes, rhodamines, a benzoxadiazole, a single-benzene-based donor-acceptor dye, an aggregation-induced emission (AIE) luminogen, and cyanines, against a fixed dose of pSiNPs (0.2 mg/mL) over a 0–100 µM concentration range, recording every fluorophore at its own excitation maximum. Quenching was strongly fluorophore-dependent, ranging from near-complete loss (fluorescein and 2′,7′-dichlorofluorescein (DCF), approximately 90%) to almost none (rose bengal (RB), approximately 4%; sulforhodamine 101 (SR 101), approximately 9%). Within the xanthene family, the extent of quenching decreased monotonically as the anionic charge density and halogen bulk increased (fluorescein < eosin Y < RB), and the same trend was observed for the rhodamines upon sulfonation. A spin-down assay that separates particle-associated dye from free dye showed that the discriminating variable is physical access to the pore: SR 101 and RB stayed almost entirely in the supernatant with low loading yields, whereas indocyanine green at 10 µM was efficiently internalized (77% loading yield) and strongly quenched. At 100 μM, the same dye self-aggregated into larger, red-shifted, self-quenched species that were excluded from the pores and therefore retained their supernatant fluorescence. Taken together, pSiNP-induced quenching is governed by charge, steric bulk, and concentration-dependent aggregation rather than by chromophore class alone, and SR 101 and RB emerge as promising candidates for pSiNP-based fluorescence applications, warranting further evaluation in biological settings.

title: Polymer-Matrix Regulation Enables Deep-Red/Near-Infrared Emission with High Fluorescence Efficiency Beyond the Crystalline State in Thiophene Sulfone AIEgens
authors: Xiaobo He; Wenjing Zhao; Xinyue Han; Xi Zhang; Ru Bai; Haoyang Wang; Yiwei Zheng; Xuebo Chen; Rui Liu; Yongqiang Dong
abstract: Abstract Achieving deep-red/near-infrared (DR/NIR) emission alongside a high fluorescence quantum yield (ΦF) in aggregation-induced emission luminogens (AIEgens) remains challenging, as the strong intramolecular charge transfer (ICT) required for long-wavelength emission typically exacerbates nonradiative decay. Herein, two donor–acceptor–donor (D–A–D) AIEgens featuring thiophene sulfone as the acceptor core are designed and synthesized to investigate the cooperative regulation of their emission behaviors by molecular structure and solid-state microenvironment. Although increasing the donor strength enables DR/NIR emission, the conventional crystalline state proves suboptimal for OTPA-α-TPS with strong ICT character, affording a limited ΦF of 27.3%. Screening of different polymer matrices reveals that polystyrene (PS) provides an ideal local microenvironment combining low polarity, rigid confinement in the glassy state, and conformational compatibility, thereby effectively restricting excited-state conformational relaxation and suppressing nonradiative decay. Consequently, the OTPA-α-TPS@PS film exhibits red-shifted emission at 685 nm with a high ΦF of 69.8%, markedly outperforming its crystalline counterpart. Furthermore, water-dispersible nanoparticles derived from OTPA-α-TPS show good cytocompatibility and enable high-contrast cellular fluorescence imaging. These findings demonstrate that an appropriate polymer microenvironment can achieve a more favorable balance between long-wavelength emission and ΦF than crystalline confinement for AIEgens with strong ICT character.
